questions.stem: Which set lists the key groups of a balanced diet?

options.text: Carbohydrate, protein, lipid, dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and water
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Three groups cannot cover the diet.
Salt is not one of the seven named groups.
Sugar is not a separate key group here.
Malnutrition is dietary, not genetic.

options.text: The health problems caused by an unbalanced diet
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Eating too much of every group
options.explanation: Malnutrition covers both excess and shortage.
Water shortage is one cause among many.

questions.stem: Why does proportion matter more than abundance in a balanced diet?

options.text: Because all groups taste better mixed
options.explanation: Taste is irrelevant to the definition.

options.text: Because the body stores every group equally
options.explanation: Groups are handled quite differently by the body.

options.text: Each group has a job, and excess of one cannot replace another group's function
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Cost is not the biological issue.

questions.stem: Which statement about the malnutrition table is correct?

options.text: It ranks foods by energy content
options.explanation: Energy ranking is a different table.
The table covers malnutrition generally.
Quantities belong to the requirements topic.

options.text: It pairs dietary causes with the health effects they produce
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A diet lacking dietary fibre mainly affects which system?

options.text: The intestine, which needs the bulk to move food along
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is vitamin A's role.
That is calcium and vitamin D.
That is iron's role.

questions.modelAnswer: A diet that includes all food groups in the correct proportions for health.

questions.stem: Name the condition caused by an unbalanced diet.
questions.modelAnswer: That condition is malnutrition, which brings a variety of health problems.

questions.stem: Explain why no single food group can sustain health alone.
questions.modelAnswer: Because each group performs a different job — energy, growth, insulation, bulk, regulation and reaction medium — and none of them covers another's function, so leaving a group out starves the body of that job no matter how much of the others is eaten.

questions.stem: A friend eats only protein shakes and rice. Use the balanced-diet idea to advise them.
questions.modelAnswer: Their diet omits lipid, vitamins, minerals, fibre and most water sources, so it is unbalanced and risks malnutrition; they should add vegetables, fruits, oils and dairy or fish to restore all seven groups in proportion.

questions.stem: Which nutrient's function is insulation and energy storage?

options.explanation: Fibre provides intestinal bulk.

options.text: Lipid, from sources such as butter, oil and nuts
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Carbohydrate is the quick energy source.
Protein builds and repairs.

questions.stem: Which mineral ion helps blood to clot and strengthens teeth and bones?

options.explanation: Vitamin C is a vitamin, not a mineral ion, and serves collagen.
Vitamin A serves the retina's pigment.

options.text: Calcium, found in milk, cheese and eggs
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Iron builds haemoglobin for oxygen transport.

questions.stem: Which vitamin or mineral shortage pairs with its condition correctly?

options.explanation: Scurvy follows vitamin C shortage.

options.text: Vitamin C shortage leading to osteoporosis
options.explanation: Osteoporosis links to long-term calcium shortage.
Anaemia follows iron shortage.

options.text: Vitamin D shortage leading to rickets in children
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

questions.stem: Why do children need a higher proportion of protein than adults?

options.text: Protein is required for growth, which is rapid in childhood
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Protein is not stored for insulation.
Adults digest protein normally.
Blood loss is not the daily driver of protein need.

questions.stem: Why does pregnancy raise energy requirements?

options.explanation: Breastfeeding comes after birth.

options.text: The developing fetus needs energy to grow, and the mother carries extra mass
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The mother breathes faster at rest
options.explanation: Breathing rate is not the stated cause.

options.text: The fetus filters the mother's blood
options.explanation: The placenta handles exchange, not the fetus directly.

questions.stem: State the function of dietary fibre.
questions.modelAnswer: Fibre provides the bulk that helps the intestine push food through.

questions.stem: Name the pigment that iron helps to build.
questions.modelAnswer: Iron builds the haemoglobin pigment that red blood cells use to carry oxygen.

questions.stem: Explain why vitamin D and calcium are often discussed together.
questions.modelAnswer: Because vitamin D enables the body to absorb calcium, so even a calcium-rich diet fails when vitamin D is lacking; both are needed for strong bones and teeth, and shortages of either can damage bone health.

questions.stem: A breastfeeding mother plans her meals. Which adjustments does the corpus guidance imply?
questions.modelAnswer: She should raise her energy intake, since breastfeeding demands extra energy, and keep calcium levels up because calcium feeds the production of rich breast milk.
